Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-06-24
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (BlueWave - Lead ML Eng), Priya Nair (BlueWave - Platform Eng), Sam Wu (BlueWave - CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
- Reviewed week 2 pilot metrics: throughput, average token latency, and queue depth.
- Identified need to bump concurrency target and tune continuous batching window for 2st/3rd tranche traffic.
- Plan to run an extended steady-state test and share detailed CSVs.

Topics covered:
- Current pilot telemetry (p95/p99, avg token lat)
- Continuous batching parameters and tradeoffs
- Concurrency target changes (per-GPU and per-route)
- Queueing/backpressure and graceful degradation rules
- KV cache priming and sequence length distribution effects
- Next steps and benchmarks to run

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick check — is this still a good time?
[00:07] Jordan: yes, we're good. just fyi we had one overnight test that blew past the earlier throughput numbers, so excited to dig in.
[00:14] Maya: awesome—i pulled the dashboards and the steadyflow run between 02:00-06:00 shows the same tail but much higher average qps. i also exported a few samples of response latency.
[00:24] Priya: i can share the traffic shape — it's spiky, short bursts from our user batch jobs, not a smooth rps. so queuing is a big factor.
[00:33] Alex: perfect. today we want to validate a few hypotheses: 1) current batching window is too conservative for the burst shape; 2) concurrency per-GPU needs to move up to meet target; 3) backpressure config should trigger earlier to avoid head-of-line latency.
[00:50] Jordan: quick clarifying q — when you say batching window conservative, do you mean the 20ms target? we saw batching waiting up to 30ms in certain flows.
[00:58] Maya: yeah, for the pilot we set a 20ms micro-batch wait to prioritise p95 but given your bursty qps we should consider moving to 30-40ms and increase concurrency so steady-state latency doesn't regress. there was also an issue with the K V cache warmup for long conversations — some tokens missed cache and spiked latency. (note: K V cache sometimes transcribed as K V cash)
[01:18] Sam: if we increase the window to 40ms won't that hurt tail latency for interactive users? our SLAs need p95 under 200ms.
[01:27] Maya: good point. the tradeoff is token-latency vs token-efficiency. with a slightly larger window paired with more concurrency you get better throughput per dollar but p95 can move a bit. the plan is to set a concurrency cap and adaptive window: aggressive during bursts, conservative during interactive paths.
[01:42] Alex: to ground this — we ran a small test yesterday with window=35ms and concurrency=8 and saw average tokens/sec improve 18% but p95 rose ~30ms, p99 rose 70ms. Jordan, do you remember the exact CSV?
[01:55] Jordan: i have it; i'll upload, but fyi the tokens/sec uplift was more obvious for shorter seqs — the long seq samples still dominated cost.
[02:03] Priya: long seqs are 10% of traffic but consume 50% of GPU cycles, so if we can isolate them to a fallback model or different route that could help.
[02:12] Maya: yes, routing long sequences to a lower-cost variant (or model with KV-friendly quant) helps. we also discussed prefix caching—if we can prime the K V cache for known repeated prompts we'll avoid cold miss spikes.
[02:25] Alex: ok let's step through metrics. Maya, can you walk the p95/p99 trends you observed?
[02:32] Maya: sure. so here's the quick read: baseline (window=20ms, concurrency=6) — p95 token latency ~185ms, p99 ~320ms. change to (window=35ms, concurrency=8) — p95 ~215ms, p99 ~390ms BUT throughput went from 420 tps to 495 tps. avg GPU util jumped ~12%. we also saw queue depth move from average 2 to 6 in peaks.
[03:02] Jordan: those numbers match what we saw, except our p95 hit 240ms in one of the mid tests, maybe due to a KV miss burst.
[03:10] Maya: yep, and i suspect that's because the cache TTL and eviction were conservative; warmup during burst didn't keep up.
[03:18] Sam: is there a way to force-evict or pre-warm certain prefixes? i can send a list of top-50 prompts.
[03:24] Priya: we'll do that. we have an internal list of common system prompts and the user prompts that repeat.
[03:29] Maya: perfect. those would help a lot. also note that continuous batching has two knobs: wait-window and max-batch-size. we kept max-batch-size low to protect latency. increasing it helps throughput at cost of per-request latency.
[03:45] Alex: what's your acceptable cost tradeoff, Sam? do you want to prioritise cost per 1k tokens or strict tail latency?
[03:52] Sam: cost matters — we have a mid-market PLG motion and we need predictable latency. i'd say p95 < 250ms is acceptable for most routes, p99 we'd like < 500ms. price needs to stay within a 20% uplift from our baseline.
[04:05] Jordan: and also for internal batch jobs we can accept higher p95 if throughput is much better — those are background. so routing matters.
[04:12] Maya: great — that gives us SLO targets to test to. I propose a two-route setup: interactive route with window=15ms, concurrency cap=4, fallback to hosted smaller model for spikes; batch route with window=40ms, concurrency=10, and aggressive batching. we'll simulate mixed traffic and measure.
[04:30] Priya: are there any recommended backpressure thresholds? we saw heap queueing where requests stack up and p99 explodes.
[04:36] Maya: yes, we suggest two levels: soft limit where queue growth triggers early batch flush and a hard limit that returns a 429-fallback to a lower-cost model or queued retry. soft around queue depth 8-10, hard at 25 for pilot config.
[04:50] Alex: also note there's a new fallback policy in the console — it can route to a quantized variant automatically when latency passes threshold; that's useful for burst protection without full 429.
[04:59] Sam: does that affect output quality? we have certain evaluators that expect stable output.
[05:05] Maya: there is some delta, yes. the quantized variant had minor token drop that our eval suite caught. we can tighten rollback rules to run A/B for a small percentage first.
[05:16] Jordan: for the steady-state run, what synthetic workload should we use? our production has short bursts (10-30s) with 2x baseline qps and then valleys.
[05:24] Maya: we'll use a mixed Poisson generator — bursts of 25-30s at 2.5x baseline, with long-tail long-seq traffic injected at 10% ratio. we'll also include priming requests to warm K V cache.
[05:36] Alex: action check — Maya will share the numeric CSVs and config diff. Jordan will give traffic traces and the top prompt list. Priya will prep VPC peering for the on-prem trial.
[05:46] Priya: one question — for the on-prem run do you need any kernel-level tuning or are we using your standard runtime bundle?
[05:53] Maya: for the initial on-prem we use the standard runtime bundle but we'll enable optimized kernels for your GPU type if you accept a small restart window. we might need to change cudnn flags and kernel selection which requires a deployment window.
[06:05] Sam: fine, we can coordinate a maintenance window.
[06:08] Jordan: small note — we saw some transcription weirdness in the logs, the "K V cache" was sometimes captured as "K V cash" in the analytics pipeline, not a blocker but noisy.
[06:16] Alex: good to know. Maya, anything else on tuning?
[06:19] Maya: yes, one more: concurrency targets are per-worker; if you're seeing head-of-line blocking, you may want to add per-route weight so that long sequences don't grab full concurrency. we can set a route weighting in the pilot.
[06:31] Jordan: ok, next question — what's the easiest path to measure real cost delta for the pilot? we need a dollar-per-1m-token estimate for each config.
[06:38] Alex: we'll produce a cost model spreadsheet with estimated GPU-hours and quantization impact. expect initial numbers in the updated pilot docs I send.
[06:46] Priya: and can you also annotate which runs used burst capacity (dedicated vs hosted) — we want to see committed cost vs burst cost.
[06:52] Maya: yes, we'll mark those. the pilot used a small dedicated pool and default hosted fallback. the spreadsheet will label per-run allocation.
[07:00] Sam: good. any blockers for the week?
[07:03] Jordan: firewall for the on-prem peering — i put a ticket in but it needs an ARN from your side for the peering policy.
[07:10] Alex: i'll get that to Priya after the call.
[07:12] Maya: last thing — i'd recommend we run two steady-state tests: one that mirrors peak bursts for 4 hours and one long tail 24-hour run at lower qps to check eviction patterns in KV cache.
[07:24] Sam: 24-hour run sounds good. we can do that over weekend.
[07:28] Alex: excellent. to recap: Maya sends CSV/config diff; Jordan uploads traffic traces and top prompts; Priya readies peering creds; Alex shares pricing delta and pilot doc. we'll reconvene next week same time to review steady-state numbers.
[07:45] Jordan: thanks everyone.
[07:47] Priya: thanks.
[07:48] Maya: thanks, bye.
